chapter: Hopkins, the South and Stuff Smith
title: Hospitalized, he loses the Safari Room job to Claude Hopkins
summary: He went into the hospital and left Hopkins in charge; the contract proved to be in Hopkins's name, and Autrey was cut out; he later worked with Hopkins again without a word.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: SO what happened?

So we started playing, and the people liked it, and we made the people like it, and we played, and entertained them, and they were very, very happy, and this particular time I started -- I got ill. I had to rush -- be rushed to the hospital. I got a -- I could not pass my water. So the doctor said come in the hospital, you need an operation, so into the hospital I went, and I asked Claude, I said well take over for me until I come out, and so and so and so. I said I'm paying him this and that, and he knew what he was getting. I said collect the money. The money is such and so. And oh, I told the manager, I said well, this was on my day off, and I say you know what your promise was. If we did -- he say yes, you did it. You've done it. He said, so the raise, and things, and you will get it. He said but the boss is out now, and -- in the Mediterranean, and when I get in touch with him, or when he comes in, I'll tell him, and tell -- quote your price to me and I'll tell him, and I'm sure he'll be agreeable. You know?
And we shook hands on it, he said well I'm sure that will be all right. so I passed the thing on to Claude, and I went into the hospital, and --
Did Claude get a trumpet player to replace you?

Yeah, I told him to get somebody to replace me, because -- because of what was happening, so when the boss, the big man did come, he had somebody to call. He had his secretary to call me, and call -- I had a phone in my room in the hospital, and then, Mr. Autrey, Mr. McClosky, the boss wanted to know, do you need anything? Whatever, you may have it. All you have to do is mention. So and so and so and so.

So I said well, thank you. And I started thinking and I said well, so many guys have been in my position and they start bugging and begging the boss for this and this, and he -- I said to myself, I won't do it. I'll show him that I'm a man, I mean, you know. And I said oh, well thank you very much, but should I need anything I will let you know, and we'll leave it like that (unintelligible).

And she said well just let us know. And I stayed there, what, thirty days? Almost, or something that way, about. Anyway, so the doctor told me, said that okay, you can go back to work next week, if you want to. I called. I said well I'm calling it, you know. I'm -- the doctor said
I could come back to work. Oh yeah? Well you -- I called the union, and they called, well you -- did you talk to Claude Hopkins? I said no, why should I? Should I? I said well I will call him then.

Well, well you talk to him. Whatever Claude says is -- so the manager says all right with me, and I got the manager, I got the union man, and finally, he said while you (unintelligible). And I said look, man, I've been in the union 40 years, and I'm supposed to call you, and I don't care where you -- what you're doing, you're supposed to take care of my business for me, you know, I know that.

And well, I said what I want to know from you is, is my contract still good? Is there another contract? Well, uh, well uh, well yes. I said well why? Who's -- I said well tell me this, is it in Claude's name? Well, yes, I think so. So okay.
: In Claude's name.

So I called Claude. I said man, I don't know what's happening. You'll have to talk to them. They won't tell you. Everybody started passing the buck. So I got him around, so sorted what was going on, and I had been had, so I turned it over to them, and (unintelligible) and this and that and that and that and that, and just and that was, and this and this and the other, so when the thing went down, Herman was still left waiting, wanting.
So okay, so the whole union, everybody heard about it thought it was the dirtiest thing they ever heard of, you know? And --
Have you seen Claude since?
Oh, yeah, I've worked with him since then.
You've worked with him?!
Yes, on a couple of jobs. Somebody booked him, and we got on the job, I was there and he was there, so he started looking me -- ducking, you know.
(Laughter.)
But I didn't say much to him. I had I wasn't going to- made up my mind (unintelligible). Why? You know, I mean why should I? I mean --
Just let bygones be bygones.
Well yeah, but I thought like hell, I mean you know.
I remember a record that Claude made, I don't think you were on it, called 'Safari Blues.' Does that come out of that room? The Safari Room?
It could have been. 'Safari Blues,' yeah.
It's a nice little riff, too.
I haven't heard of it.
Catchy little riff, very nice.
I bet you -- no, no. I don't know. So
